title: Premature Microservices
description: Splitting a system into services before the organization or domain is ready, producing a distributed monolith.

sections.overview: A team adopts microservices while it is small, the domain is still changing, or the platform cannot yet support many services. The result has the operational costs of a distributed system without independent deployability.
causes: Copying the architecture of much larger companies.
Treating 'scale' as a reason when the bottleneck is elsewhere.
Boundaries drawn by technical layer (users service, email service) instead of business capability.
progression: A handful of services share a database and a release.
Features require changes in several services at once.
Local development needs many services running.
Incidents involve chains of calls nobody can trace.
warningSigns: Most features touch three or more services.
No distributed tracing, yet many network hops.
technicalImpact: Latency and partial failure from network calls.
Data consistency problems across service databases.
organizationalImpact: Engineers spend time on plumbing instead of product.
prevention: Extract a service only with a named benefit (independent release, scaling, isolation) and an owning team.
Have deployment automation and tracing before the second service.
recovery: Merge tightly coupled services back into one deployable.
Invest in tracing to find the chattiest paths first.
sections.summary: Distribution is a cost you pay for team independence. Without that need, it is pure cost.

relations.note: Chatty synchronous call chains spread failure.
A key risk to check for in early-stage companies.

title: Premature Kubernetes
description: Adopting Kubernetes before the workload or team needs it, so platform work crowds out product work. Also: when Kubernetes becomes a liability.

sections.overview: A small team runs a handful of services on Kubernetes and spends a large share of its time on clusters, add-ons, YAML and upgrades instead of the product.
causes: Choosing Kubernetes as the default without comparing simpler platforms.
Expecting future scale that has not arrived.
progression: Initial setup takes weeks.
Add-ons accumulate (ingress, cert-manager, autoscaler, secrets operator).
Upgrades are postponed.
One engineer becomes the cluster expert.
warningSigns: Fewer than ~10 services on a dedicated cluster.
Cluster versions approaching end of support.
Only one person can debug the cluster.
businessImpact: Staff cost exceeding the infrastructure it manages.
prevention: Start on ECS/Fargate, Cloud Run or a PaaS.
Adopt Kubernetes when service count, ecosystem needs or portability justify it, with a named owner.
recovery: Move to a managed control plane at minimum.
Introduce a golden path that hides cluster details.
Consider migrating simple services to a managed container platform.
sections.summary: Kubernetes becomes a liability when the team spends more effort running it than it saves.

relations.note: Cluster knowledge concentrates in one person.
A common source of operational debt.

title: Over-Sharding
description: Partitioning data earlier or more finely than necessary, making queries, transactions and operations harder.

sections.overview: Data is split across many shards before a single database was the bottleneck, or with a shard key that does not match access patterns.
causes: Choosing a shard key without analysing queries.
progression: Cross-shard queries appear for common features.
Transactions span shards.
Rebalancing and schema changes become multi-day operations.
businessImpact: Slower feature delivery; higher database cost.
prevention: Exhaust vertical scaling, indexing, caching and replicas first.
Choose shard keys from real access patterns.
recovery: Move to a distributed SQL database that handles partitioning.
sections.summary: Shard late, coarsely, and on the right key.

relations.note: Vertical scaling often postpones sharding for years.

title: Over-Abstraction
description: Layers of frameworks, platforms or patterns that hide what the system does and slow every change.

sections.overview: Abstractions are added for flexibility that is never used: generic platforms, multi-cloud wrappers, plugin systems, event sourcing for CRUD. Engineers must understand the abstraction and the thing underneath.
progression: Simple changes require touching several layers.
Debugging requires reading framework internals.
Teams bypass the abstraction, leaving two ways to do everything.
warningSigns: New hires take weeks to make a first change.
prevention: Abstract after the third concrete case, not before.
Measure the path from idea to production.
recovery: Document and support the direct path.

relations.note: Golden paths should guide, not hide.
Ask what the abstraction is for.

title: Single Point of Failure
description: A component whose failure alone takes down the system.

sections.overview: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component, dependency, person or process without redundancy whose failure causes an outage.
causes: Shared dependencies (DNS, identity, configuration, a CDN) that everything relies on.
Global configuration pushes that reach everywhere at once.
One person who knows how to recover a system.
progression: Systems grow around an assumed-reliable dependency.
The dependency's failure mode is never tested.
It fails and takes everything with it.
warningSigns: Components with 'we've never had a problem with it'.
Changes deployed globally in one step.
prevention: Staged rollouts of configuration and code.
sections.summary: Find SPOFs on purpose, including people and processes.

relations.note: SPOF failures propagate to every dependent.
A global configuration push acted as a single point of failure in Cloudflare's 2019 outage.

title: Cascade Failures
description: A failure in one component overloads or blocks others, spreading until large parts of the system are down.
problems: how do I avoid cascading failures
one slow service takes everything down

sections.overview: A cascade failure grows through positive feedback: a slow dependency ties up callers' threads or connections, callers slow down, their callers time out and retry, and load concentrates on the remaining healthy capacity until it also fails.
causes: Load shifting to fewer healthy instances after a partial failure.
progression: Latency rises in one dependency.
Thread pools and connection pools fill.
Health checks fail and instances are removed, concentrating load.
Retries amplify load; the system collapses.
warningSigns: Rising latency followed by rising error rates in callers.
technicalImpact: Slow recovery because restarted instances are overwhelmed.
businessImpact: Major incidents and long recovery time.
organizationalImpact: Incident response across many teams at once.
prevention: Retry budgets with backoff and jitter.
Capacity headroom for losing a zone.
sections.summary: Design every call path for its dependency being slow, not just down.

relations.note: Recovery attempts can cause a herd.

title: Retry Storms
description: Retries multiplying traffic against an already struggling service, preventing it from recovering.

sections.overview: When each layer in a call chain retries failed requests, load multiplies. Three layers retrying three times can turn one request into 27 at the bottom of the stack.
causes: Retries at several layers (client, gateway, mesh, service).
progression: A dependency slows.
Callers time out and retry.
Traffic to the dependency multiplies.
It cannot recover until retries stop.
warningSigns: Request rate at a dependency exceeding user traffic during incidents.
Retry metrics climbing together with errors.
technicalImpact: Prolonged outages; recovery requires manual load shedding.
recovery: Disable retries or open circuit breakers.

title: Thundering Herd
description: Many clients act at the same moment (cache expiry, reconnect, failover) and overwhelm a shared resource.

sections.overview: A thundering herd occurs when a synchronized event causes many clients to hit the same resource simultaneously: a popular cache key expires, a service restarts and all clients reconnect, or traffic fails over to a cold region.
causes: Cold caches after deploys or failovers.
Scheduled jobs all starting on the hour.
progression: Synchronized trigger.
Burst far above normal load.
Backend saturates; errors trigger retries; the herd grows.
warningSigns: Load spikes aligned with cache TTLs or cron schedules.
Errors immediately after deploys or failovers.
technicalImpact: Short, intense overloads that can trigger cascades.
organizationalImpact: Fear of deploys and failover drills.
prevention: Jitter on TTLs, retries and schedules.
sections.summary: Randomize anything many clients do at once.

relations.note: A herd can push a system into a cascade.

title: Secret Sprawl
description: Credentials scattered across code, config files, CI variables, images and chat, with no inventory or rotation.

sections.overview: Secrets are copied wherever they are needed. Nobody knows how many copies exist, who has access, or what breaks if one is rotated.
progression: Secrets in environment files and CI.
Copies in images and logs.
Rotation becomes too risky to attempt.
warningSigns: Secret scanners finding credentials in repositories.
technicalImpact: Broad access after a single leak.
recovery: Migrate consumers to the secrets manager.

title: Exposed Buckets
description: Object storage made publicly readable or writable by misconfiguration, exposing sensitive data.

sections.overview: Buckets are opened for convenience (sharing, static hosting) or through overly broad policies, and sensitive data ends up publicly accessible.
causes: Mixing public assets and private data in one bucket.
No guardrails at the account level.
prevention: Block public access at the account level by default.
Serve public content through a CDN with private origins.
sections.summary: Private by default; public only through deliberate, reviewed paths.

relations.note: Least-privilege access applies to data stores too.

title: Ownership Confusion
description: Services, data, topics or infrastructure without a clear owning team.
problems: my engineering team is struggling with service ownership
nobody knows who owns this service

sections.overview: When nobody clearly owns a component, it does not get upgraded, alerts go nowhere, and incidents start with 'who owns this?'.
causes: Shared components (topics, schemas, libraries) owned by 'everyone'.
progression: Alerts are muted.
Dependencies fall behind.
Incidents take longer because responders are unclear.
warningSigns: Pages routed to a generic channel.
prevention: A service catalog with an owning team for every component.
Ownership transfer as part of reorganizations.
sections.summary: Every component needs a team, a pager and a catalog entry.

relations.note: Unclear ownership often coexists with concentrated knowledge.

title: Platform Team Bottleneck
description: A central platform or infrastructure team becomes a queue that every product team waits on.

sections.overview: Product teams must file tickets for environments, deployments or permissions. The platform team is overloaded, and delivery speed across the company drops.
causes: No product management for the platform.
progression: Ticket queues grow.
Teams build shadow infrastructure to get around them.
Standards erode.
warningSigns: Lead time dominated by waiting on another team.
organizationalImpact: Friction between platform and product teams.
prevention: Treat the platform as a product with users and metrics.
Clear interfaces between platform and product responsibilities.
recovery: Automate the most common ticket types.
Embed platform engineers temporarily with heavy users.
sections.summary: Platforms should remove waiting, not create it.

relations.note: Self-service paths are the main fix.

title: Knowledge Silos
description: Critical operational or design knowledge held by one person or a small group.
problems: only one person knows how to deploy

sections.overview: Specialist systems and undocumented processes concentrate knowledge. When that person is unavailable, incidents last longer and changes stall.
causes: Specialist infrastructure run by one expert.
progression: The expert handles every incident.
Others avoid the system.
The expert leaves or burns out.
warningSigns: The same name on every incident.
prevention: Rotation of on-call and change ownership.
Prefer managed services over specialist self-hosted systems.
recovery: Document while the expert is still available.
sections.summary: If only one person can fix it, it is a single point of failure.

relations.note: People can be single points of failure.
